h1: The 7 Best Ultrawide Monitors With USB-C for a One-Cable Desk, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Ultrawide Monitors USB-C: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 ultrawide monitors with USB-C scored on power delivery, panel type, refresh rate, ports, KVM and warranty.
summary: The Dell UltraSharp U3425WE is the USB-C ultrawide to buy if you want the full one-cable desk, with Thunderbolt 4, an IPS panel at 120Hz and ten USB ports. The Dell U4924DW is the 49 inch option, the Philips 346B1C adds a built-in KVM at a lower price, and the Samsung ViewFinity S65UA offers 90W charging for big laptops.
intro: The trap with USB-C monitors is the number printed next to the port. A laptop that needs 90W will charge slowly or not at all from a 65W port, and some monitors list USB-C data and video without making clear how much power flows back. Before you look at refresh rate or panel type, match the monitor's power delivery to your laptop's charger.

This ranking starts with the cable: power delivery, docking features and ports. It then looks at panel type, refresh rate, size and warranty. We reviewed seven ultrawide monitors from their listings and spec sheets, and we do not credit a feature the listing leaves out.

products.name: Dell UltraSharp U3425WE
products.verdict: A 34 inch IPS with Thunderbolt 4, ten USB 3.2 Gen2 ports and Ethernet in one box.
products.description:
The U3425WE is a 34 inch IPS ultrawide at 3440x1440 and 120Hz. It is the only Thunderbolt 4 monitor in this ranking, with ten USB 3.2 Gen2 ports in total, Ethernet, picture-by-picture, an ambient light sensor and G-Sync compatibility, under a 3-year warranty.

It wins because it turns the monitor into a proper dock. Thunderbolt 4 carries video, data and power through one cable, and the port count lets a laptop plug into a keyboard, drives and a network without a separate hub. IPS panels also hold their colors from the side better than the VA panels used by most rivals here. The price is the catch: it sits in the $500 and up bracket, and some of that cost pays for features a simple home setup will not touch.

Buy it if you work from one laptop and want a single-cable desk that lasts. Skip it if you do not need Thunderbolt or this many ports.
cons: More ports than casual users need
products.idealFor: Remote workers who dock one laptop daily.
products.skipIf: You only need a basic USB-C connection.

products.name: Dell UltraSharp U4924DW
products.verdict: A 49 inch, 5120x1440 IPS Black monitor with 90W USB-C, KVM and 2.5GbE.
products.description:
The U4924DW is a 49 inch IPS Black monitor at 5120x1440, the widest panel here. It has 90W USB-C power delivery, an automatic KVM switch, 2.5GbE Ethernet, 11 USB ports in total, dual 9W speakers and 100% sRGB coverage.

It ranks second because a 49 inch screen is effectively two 27 inch panels without a bezel in the middle, which suits traders, coders and anyone who wants side-by-side documents. The automatic KVM lets one keyboard and mouse control two computers, a feature the 34 inch Dell lacks. The cost is desk space and money: a 49 inch curve needs a deep, wide desk, and the price lands in the $500 and up bracket. At 1440 pixels tall it also has the same vertical resolution as the 34 inch models.

Buy it if you want the ultimate wide workspace and have the desk. Skip it if your desk is under about 55 inches wide.
products.idealFor: Power users who want two screens in one.

products.name: Philips 346B1C
products.verdict: The only 34 inch pick with a built-in KVM switch, plus 95W USB-C and Gigabit Ethernet.
products.description:
The Philips 346B1C is a 34 inch VA ultrawide at 3440x1440 and 100Hz. It has 95W USB-C power delivery, a built-in KVM switch, a Gigabit Ethernet port, 119% sRGB and 90% Adobe RGB coverage, and a 4-year advance replacement warranty.

It takes third place because it hands you the strongest charging in the group at 95W while including a KVM in the $200 to $500 bracket. If you share a keyboard and mouse between a work laptop and a personal PC, the KVM saves you a switch box. The 4-year advance replacement warranty is the best coverage here, because a replacement ships before you send yours back. The tradeoff against the IPS Dells is the VA panel, which has deeper blacks but narrower viewing angles.

It is a strong buy for hybrid workers juggling two computers. Skip it if you want an IPS panel or Thunderbolt.
pros: 95W USB-C is the strongest at 34 inches
cons: VA panel has narrower viewing angles
products.idealFor: Hybrid workers sharing one keyboard across two PCs.

products.name: Samsung ViewFinity S65UA
products.verdict: A 1000R curved 34 inch with 90W USB-C, Ethernet and HDR10 for a mid-range price.
products.description:
The ViewFinity S65UA is a 34 inch, 1000R curved VA monitor at 3440x1440 and 100Hz. It provides 90W USB-C power delivery, HDR10 support, a built-in Ethernet port, TUV-certified eye care and a 3-year warranty.

It places fourth because it gives you 90W charging, a strong figure that covers most large laptops, plus Ethernet in the $200 to $500 bracket. The 1000R curve is the tightest of the group and wraps around your field of view, which many users like for immersion and some find a bit much for spreadsheets. HDR10 is a label more than a showpiece on a VA panel without local dimming. It lacks the KVM of the Philips and the speed of the Dell S3425DW.

Buy it if your laptop wants 90W and you like a strong curve. Skip it if you want a KVM.
cons: HDR10 limited on this panel type
products.idealFor: Users charging a 90W laptop who like a deep curve.
products.skipIf: You want a flatter screen or a KVM.

products.name: Dell 34 Plus USB-C Curved Monitor (S3425DW)
products.verdict: A 34 inch curved VA with up to 120Hz, 0.03ms response and 65W USB-C.
products.description:
The S3425DW is a 34 inch curved VA monitor at 3440x1440 and up to 120Hz. It lists a 0.03ms response time, the fastest here, with 65W USB-C power delivery, 99% sRGB, 95% DCI-P3 and 3000:1 contrast. It has built-in speakers and Dell's Premium Panel warranty.

It ranks fifth because speed and color are strong, but the 65W USB-C limits it for large laptops, and it has no Ethernet or KVM. For an ultrabook that draws well under 65W, that is fine. The 120Hz refresh gives smoother scrolling and gaming than the 100Hz rivals, and the 95% DCI-P3 coverage suits photo and video work. The 3000:1 contrast is the VA advantage, with deeper blacks than IPS in a dim room.

Buy it for mixed work and play with a light laptop. Skip it if you need more than 65W.
products.idealFor: Mixed work and gaming with a light laptop.

products.name: Philips 34E1C5600HE
products.verdict: A 34 inch curved VA with a 5MP Windows Hello webcam, mic and a 4-year warranty.
products.description:
The Philips 34E1C5600HE is a 34 inch curved VA monitor at 3440x1440 and 100Hz. It has 65W USB-C power delivery, a built-in 5MP webcam with Windows Hello and a noise-canceling mic, dual 5W speakers and a 4-year advance replacement warranty.

It ranks sixth because the webcam is its identity. For video calls it removes the need for a separate camera, and Windows Hello gives you face login without extra hardware. The other tradeoff is power delivery: 65W suits lighter laptops only. It has no KVM or Ethernet port. A monitor webcam sits at the top of the screen, which gives a flattering call angle, but it is hard to replace if it fails, so the long warranty matters.

Buy it if you spend your day on video calls. Skip it if you already own a good webcam.
products.idealFor: People who spend hours on video calls.

products.name: LG 34WR55QK-B
products.verdict: A 34 inch curved VA with 65W USB-C, Reader Mode, PbP and a height-adjustable stand.
products.description:
The LG 34WR55QK-B is a 34 inch curved VA monitor at 3440x1440 and 100Hz. It supports 65W USB-C power delivery, Reader Mode, picture-by-picture, OnScreen Control software and a stand with height and tilt adjustment.

It ranks last because the spec sheet stops at the basics: no KVM, no Ethernet, no stated warranty detail and only 65W of charging. That does not make it a poor monitor; it makes it the plainest. Reader Mode softens the display's blue light, and OnScreen Control lets you split windows with a few clicks. A height-adjustable stand is a real convenience that some rivals leave out.

Buy it if you want the simplest USB-C ultrawide and a clean setup. Skip it if you need docking features.
products.idealFor: People who want a plain USB-C ultrawide.
products.skipIf: You want a docking hub built in.

methodology.title: USB-C power and docking
methodology.description: We compared wattage from 65W to 95W, Thunderbolt 4 support, and built-in Ethernet and KVM, since those decide how much a single cable can do.

methodology.title: Panel type and refresh
methodology.description: IPS, IPS Black and VA panels at 100Hz and 120Hz were weighed for viewing angles, contrast and motion handling.

methodology.title: Size and resolution
methodology.description: 34 inch 3440x1440 and 49 inch 5120x1440 formats were compared for desk fit and workspace.

methodology.title: Ports and extras
methodology.description: USB port count, speakers, webcam and software features were scored for everyday usefulness.

methodology.title: Warranty and price
methodology.description: Warranty terms of 3 and 4 years, including advance replacement, were set against the $200 to $500 and $500 and up brackets.

whatMatters.detail: Power delivery is how much charge the monitor sends back to your laptop through the same cable. A thin laptop may run on 65W, while a performance model may want 90W or more. Check your charger's wattage and match or exceed it, because a lower figure may charge slowly or not while you work.

A plain USB-C port with DisplayPort Alt Mode carries video and power. Thunderbolt 4 adds higher bandwidth and daisy-chaining, and in this ranking only the Dell U3425WE offers it. Choose Thunderbolt if you plan to attach fast drives or a second display.

IPS panels hold color and brightness when you view from the side. VA panels have deeper blacks and higher contrast but narrower angles. On a curved ultrawide you sit near the center, so VA is usually acceptable for office work.

A KVM switch lets one keyboard and mouse control two computers, and a built-in Ethernet port gives a wired connection through the monitor. Both reduce desk clutter. Look for the terms KVM and RJ45 or Gigabit in the listing.
An advance replacement warranty ships a new unit before you return the old one, which keeps you working. Four years is long for a monitor. Note whether the dead-pixel policy is stated on the listing.

howToChoose.intro: USB-C wattage is the first filter, since it sets what your laptop can do from one cable.

cards.label: IPS
cards.text: Wider viewing angles and steadier colors off center, a better fit for shared screens and color work. Picks: Dell UltraSharp U3425WE, Dell UltraSharp U4924DW (IPS Black).

cards.label: VA
cards.text: Higher contrast and deeper blacks at a lower price, with weaker angles. Picks: Philips 346B1C, Samsung S65UA, Dell S3425DW, Philips 34E1C5600HE, LG 34WR55QK-B.

howToChoose.note: Default to IPS if you will share the screen or edit images; VA is fine for solo office work.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: USB-C power that matches your laptop, an Ethernet port, a KVM if you juggle work and personal machines, and a warranty of at least 3 years.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Dell UltraSharp U3425WE for full docking, the Philips 346B1C for KVM value and the Philips 34E1C5600HE for call-heavy days.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You dock daily, need Thunderbolt or want a 49 inch workspace. The Dell U3425WE and U4924DW justify the $500 and up bracket.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You just need a clean USB-C connection to a light laptop. The LG 34WR55QK-B covers it.

faq.q: Will my laptop charge through the monitor's USB-C port?
faq.a: Only if the monitor's power delivery meets your laptop's needs. A 65W port may charge an ultrabook but struggle with a 100W machine. Check your charger's wattage and pick a monitor at that level or higher.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake with USB-C monitors?
faq.a: Assuming every USB-C port carries video. Your laptop port must support DisplayPort Alt Mode or Thunderbolt for the single-cable setup. Check the laptop's spec page before buying.

faq.q: Is the Dell U3425WE worth it over the Philips 346B1C?
faq.a: If you need Thunderbolt 4, an IPS panel and ten ports, yes. If you want a KVM and strong 95W charging for less, the Philips is the better value. Neither is wrong; they serve different desks.

Connect the USB-C cable to the laptop, then attach the stand and plug in power. Set the resolution to 3440x1440 in your display settings. If the monitor has a KVM, you may need to assign inputs in the on-screen menu.

faq.q: Can I run two computers on one monitor?
faq.a: Yes, with picture-by-picture or a KVM. The Philips 346B1C and Dell UltraSharp U4924DW include KVM switching, while the Dell U3425WE and LG offer picture-by-picture to show two inputs side by side.

faq.q: Does a curved ultrawide suit gaming?
faq.a: It can, particularly at 120Hz as on the Dell S3425DW or U3425WE. A 100Hz screen still works for casual play. Check your graphics output supports the resolution at that rate.

finalTake: For a one-cable desk, the Dell UltraSharp U3425WE is the best USB-C ultrawide here, with Thunderbolt 4, IPS and a deep port list. The Philips 346B1C is the value choice with a KVM and 95W charging, and the Dell UltraSharp U4924DW is the answer for a 49 inch workspace. Match the power delivery to your laptop before you consider anything else.
